name: Silver (Crayola)
lede: Silver (Crayola) is a pale, slightly warm grey that Crayola names as a qualified variant of plain Silver, close enough to a swatch Robert Ridgway published in 1912 that the two are easy to mistake for one color.

sections.title: A Crayola qualifier
sections.body:
Our color library files this grey as a Crayola box name, kept separate from the library's plainer [[silver]] entry because it is a named qualifier rather than a duplicate [1]. Robert Ridgway's 1912 nomenclature for naturalists already carried two very close swatches, plate XLV at hue 1′′′′, tone f, and a second at hue 5′′′′, tone f; both were later classified under the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 as block 232, a pinkish gray about 2.8 units from that block's reference color [1]. Whether Ridgway's nineteenth-century grey and Crayola's twentieth-century crayon share any real history, or are simply the same pale grey arrived at twice, is not something our sources settle [1].

The nearest named colors on file, by real look-alike distance rather than any curriculum shortcut, are [[lilac-grey]] and [[pale-ecru-drab]], both almost the same hue, with the plainer [[silver]] a little further off and [[oatmeal]] more vivid still [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this grey in 555 of 23,781 paintings, about 2.33 percent, as photographed; the stricter within-painting lens counts it in 387, more common than 80 percent of the named colors we track [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light, 66 percent of those 387 appearances, by lightness rank rather than raw brightness, so varnish cannot fake it [3].

Its most devoted painter is Xugu, who used it in 5 of 16 works here, 7.1 times his own baseline [3]. The earliest match is dated 1000, with 470 dated paintings in all; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first, and it is nine hundred and twelve years before the Crayola name's own earliest record in our sources, 1912 — a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof the named grey existed that early [1][3].
